Topic 02·Anik Sir · Lecture 2

Step, impulse, exponentials and sinusoids

The step and impulse and how each builds the other, exponentials, complex exponentials, and discrete periodicity.

3 past questions on this topic

Why these signals?

A handful of simple signals appear everywhere in this course. The unit step and unit impulse are the building blocks for describing switches, pulses and systems. Exponentials and sinusoids are the building blocks for Fourier, Laplace and z-transforms. Learn their shapes and how they relate, and most later derivations become one-liners.

The discrete unit step

u[n]={0,n<01,n≥0u[n]=\begin{cases}0,&n<0\\1,&n\ge0\end{cases}u[n]={0,1,​n<0n≥0​

It is "off" for negative nnn and switches "on" at n=0n=0n=0, staying on forever. Note that u[0]=1u[0]=1u[0]=1.

The discrete unit impulse

δ[n]={1,n=00,n≠0\delta[n]=\begin{cases}1,&n=0\\0,&n\ne0\end{cases}δ[n]={1,0,​n=0n=0​

It is non-zero at exactly one instant, the origin. Think of it as a single tap: the simplest possible input.

Quick values. u[1]=1u[1]=1u[1]=1, u[−3]=0u[-3]=0u[−3]=0, u[0]=1u[0]=1u[0]=1; δ[0]=1\delta[0]=1δ[0]=1, δ[4]=0\delta[4]=0δ[4]=0, δ[−2]=0\delta[-2]=0δ[−2]=0.

Shifted steps and impulses

The rules of time shifting from the previous topic apply directly:

  • u[n−2]u[n-2]u[n−2] switches on at n=2n=2n=2 (delay by 2); u[n+3]u[n+3]u[n+3] switches on at n=−3n=-3n=−3 (advance by 3).
  • δ[n−2]\delta[n-2]δ[n−2] is a single 1 at n=2n=2n=2; δ[n+3]\delta[n+3]δ[n+3] is a single 1 at n=−3n=-3n=−3.

In general, δ[n−k]\delta[n-k]δ[n−k] is 111 exactly where n=kn=kn=k.

Three relations between step and impulse

R1 — the impulse is the first difference of the step

δ[n]=u[n]−u[n−1]\delta[n]=u[n]-u[n-1]δ[n]=u[n]−u[n−1]

Subtract the step delayed by one sample from the step itself. For n≥1n\ge1n≥1 both are 1 and cancel; for n<0n<0n<0 both are 0. Only at n=0n=0n=0 do we get 1−0=11-0=11−0=1.

R2 — the running sum of the impulse is the step

u[n]=∑m=−∞nδ[m]u[n]=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{n}\delta[m]u[n]=m=−∞∑n​δ[m]

The running sum adds every value of δ[m]\delta[m]δ[m] from −∞-\infty−∞ up to m=nm=nm=n. The only non-zero value of δ[m]\delta[m]δ[m] is at m=0m=0m=0, so the question is simply: is the spike inside the window?

  • If n<0n<0n<0, the window stops before m=0m=0m=0: the sum is 000.
  • If n≥0n\ge0n≥0, the window includes m=0m=0m=0: the sum is 111.

That is exactly u[n]u[n]u[n].

R3 — delayed impulses build the step

u[n]=δ[n]+δ[n−1]+δ[n−2]+⋯=∑k=0∞δ[n−k]\begin{aligned}&u[n]\\[6pt]&= \delta[n]+\delta[n-1]+\delta[n-2]+\cdots\\[6pt]&= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta[n-k]\end{aligned}​u[n]=δ[n]+δ[n−1]+δ[n−2]+⋯=k=0∑∞​δ[n−k]​

Each delayed impulse δ[n−k]\delta[n-k]δ[n−k] contributes exactly one sample, a 1 at n=kn=kn=k. Adding them for k=0,1,2,…k=0,1,2,\dotsk=0,1,2,… puts a 1 at every n≥0n\ge0n≥0.

R1 and R2 are the discrete versions of "differentiate" and "integrate". The first difference undoes the running sum, just as ddt\frac{d}{dt}dtd​ undoes ∫\int∫.

The continuous unit step

u(t)={0,t<01,t>0u(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t<0\\1,&t>0\end{cases}u(t)={0,1,​t<0t>0​

It jumps from 0 to 1 at t=0t=0t=0. The value exactly at t=0t=0t=0 is usually left undefined (or set to ½); it never matters in our operations.

The continuous unit impulse

In discrete time we had δ[n]=u[n]−u[n−1]\delta[n]=u[n]-u[n-1]δ[n]=u[n]−u[n−1], a difference. In continuous time we want the analogous idea, a derivative:

δ(t)=du(t)dt.\delta(t)=\frac{du(t)}{dt}.δ(t)=dtdu(t)​.

But there is a problem. Away from t=0t=0t=0 the step is flat, so its derivative is 0. At t=0t=0t=0 it jumps instantly, and the ordinary derivative does not exist there.

The fix: smooth the jump first

Replace the instant jump by a short ramp that rises from 0 to 1 over a tiny interval Δ\DeltaΔ:

uΔ(t)={0,t<0t/Δ,0≤t≤Δ1,t>Δ⇒δΔ(t)=duΔdt={1/Δ,0<t<Δ0,otherwiseu_\Delta(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t<0\\ t/\Delta,&0\le t\le\Delta\\ 1,&t>\Delta\end{cases} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \delta_\Delta(t)=\frac{du_\Delta}{dt}=\begin{cases}1/\Delta,&0<t<\Delta\\0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}uΔ​(t)=⎩⎨⎧​0,t/Δ,1,​t<00≤t≤Δt>Δ​⇒δΔ​(t)=dtduΔ​​={1/Δ,0,​0<t<Δotherwise​

The derivative is a rectangular pulse of height 1/Δ1/\Delta1/Δ and width Δ\DeltaΔ. Its area is always

∫−∞∞δΔ(t) dt=1Δ⋅Δ=1.\begin{aligned}&\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_\Delta(t)\,dt\\[6pt]&= \frac1\Delta\cdot\Delta\\[6pt]&= 1 .\end{aligned}​∫−∞∞​δΔ​(t)dt=Δ1​⋅Δ=1.​

Make the ramp steeper

As Δ\DeltaΔ shrinks, the ramp becomes steeper and the pulse becomes taller and narrower, but its area stays exactly 1. The area is the quantity that survives.

The ideal impulse δ(t)\delta(t)δ(t) is the limit of this infinitely narrow, infinitely tall pulse of unit area:

δ(t)=0  (t≠0),∫−∞∞δ(t) dt=1,\delta(t)=0\ \ (t\ne0),\qquad\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t)\,dt=1,δ(t)=0  (t=0),∫−∞∞​δ(t)dt=1, δ(t)=du(t)dt,u(t)=∫−∞tδ(τ) dτ.\delta(t)=\frac{du(t)}{dt},\qquad u(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau)\,d\tau .δ(t)=dtdu(t)​,u(t)=∫−∞t​δ(τ)dτ.

Drawing impulses

An impulse is drawn as an arrow. The arrow's height is not a value; the number beside it is the area (strength). 2δ(t−1)2\delta(t-1)2δ(t−1) is an impulse of strength 2 at t=1t=1t=1; −3δ(t−3)-3\delta(t-3)−3δ(t−3) points downward with strength 3 at t=3t=3t=3.

Example: differentiating 2u(t)2u(t)2u(t)

ddt 2u(t)=2δ(t).\frac{d}{dt}\,2u(t)=2\delta(t).dtd​2u(t)=2δ(t).

A jump of height 2 becomes an impulse of area 2.

Example: a signal with several jumps

Read the jumps of the signal below from left to right:

atfrom → tojump
t=1t=1t=10→20\to20→2+2+2+2
t=2t=2t=22→−12\to-12→−1−3-3−3
t=4t=4t=4−1→1-1\to1−1→1+2+2+2

Each jump is a scaled, shifted step, so

x(t)=2u(t−1)−3u(t−2)+2u(t−4),dxdt=2δ(t−1)−3δ(t−2)+2δ(t−4).x(t)=2u(t-1)-3u(t-2)+2u(t-4),\qquad \frac{dx}{dt}=2\delta(t-1)-3\delta(t-2)+2\delta(t-4).x(t)=2u(t−1)−3u(t−2)+2u(t−4),dtdx​=2δ(t−1)−3δ(t−2)+2δ(t−4).

Derivative of any piecewise signal = (slope of each smooth piece) + (an impulse at every jump, with strength equal to the jump: up is positive, down is negative).

Real exponentials

x(t)=Ceat,C, a real.x(t)=Ce^{at},\qquad C,\ a\ \text{real}.x(t)=Ceat,C, a real.
  • a>0a>0a>0: grows without bound.
  • a=0a=0a=0: constant at CCC.
  • a<0a<0a<0: decays toward 0.

Every curve passes through CCC at t=0t=0t=0.

The step as a switch

Multiplying by u(t)u(t)u(t) keeps the right side of a signal and removes the left side: x(t)u(t)=x(t)x(t)u(t)=x(t)x(t)u(t)=x(t) for t>0t>0t>0 and 000 for t<0t<0t<0.

Shifted and reversed steps choose where the signal turns on or off:

  • etu(−t)e^{t}u(-t)etu(−t): kept only for t≤0t\le0t≤0.
  • e−tu(t−2)e^{-t}u(t-2)e−tu(t−2): turns on at t=2t=2t=2, starting from height e−2e^{-2}e−2.
  • etu(3−t)e^{t}u(3-t)etu(3−t): kept only for t≤3t\le3t≤3; zero after 3.
  • e−tu(3t)=e−tu(t)e^{-t}u(3t)=e^{-t}u(t)e−tu(3t)=e−tu(t), because 3t3t3t has the same sign as ttt, so u(3t)=u(t)u(3t)=u(t)u(3t)=u(t).

Sinusoids

x(t)=Acos⁡(ω0t+ϕ)x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0t+\phi)x(t)=Acos(ω0​t+ϕ)
  • AAA controls the height (amplitude).
  • ω0\omega_0ω0​ controls the speed of oscillation (rad/s).
  • ϕ\phiϕ shifts the wave (phase).

One full cycle takes the fundamental period

T0=2π∣ω0∣.T_0=\frac{2\pi}{|\omega_0|}.T0​=∣ω0​∣2π​.

Larger ∣ω0∣|\omega_0|∣ω0​∣ means faster oscillation and a shorter period.

Complex exponentials: a rotating point

Picture a point moving around the unit circle. At angle θ=ω0t\theta=\omega_0tθ=ω0​t, its horizontal coordinate is cos⁡ω0t\cos\omega_0tcosω0​t and its vertical coordinate is sin⁡ω0t\sin\omega_0tsinω0​t. Both sinusoids are two views of the same rotation.

Euler's formula packages both into one expression:

ejθ=cos⁡θ+jsin⁡θ⇒ejω0t=cos⁡ω0t+jsin⁡ω0t.e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad e^{j\omega_0t}=\cos\omega_0t+j\sin\omega_0t .ejθ=cosθ+jsinθ⇒ejω0​t=cosω0​t+jsinω0​t. Re⁡{ejω0t}=cos⁡ω0t,Im⁡{ejω0t}=sin⁡ω0t.\operatorname{Re}\{e^{j\omega_0t}\}=\cos\omega_0t,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\{e^{j\omega_0t}\}=\sin\omega_0t .Re{ejω0​t}=cosω0​t,Im{ejω0​t}=sinω0​t.
  • ejω0te^{j\omega_0t}ejω0​t rotates counter-clockwise at speed ω0\omega_0ω0​.
  • ej2ω0te^{j2\omega_0t}ej2ω0​t rotates twice as fast.
  • e−jω0te^{-j\omega_0t}e−jω0​t rotates in the opposite direction.

A real cosine is two opposite rotations

cos⁡ω0t=12ejω0t+12e−jω0t,sin⁡ω0t=12j(ejω0t−e−jω0t).\cos\omega_0t=\tfrac12e^{j\omega_0t}+\tfrac12e^{-j\omega_0t},\qquad \sin\omega_0t=\frac{1}{2j}\left(e^{j\omega_0t}-e^{-j\omega_0t}\right).cosω0​t=21​ejω0​t+21​e−jω0​t,sinω0​t=2j1​(ejω0​t−e−jω0​t).

Two half-length arrows turn in opposite directions. Their imaginary parts always cancel, so their sum stays on the real axis.

These two identities are used constantly: they let us read Fourier series coefficients straight off a sinusoid without integrating.

Periodicity of ejω0te^{j\omega_0t}ejω0​t

After one full rotation the point is back where it started:

ejω0(t+T)=ejω0t  ⟺  ejω0T=1  ⟺  ω0T=2π  ⟺  T0=2π∣ω0∣.\begin{aligned}&e^{j\omega_0(t+T)}=e^{j\omega_0t}\\[6pt]&\iff e^{j\omega_0T}=1\\[6pt]&\iff \omega_0T=2\pi\\[6pt]&\iff T_0=\frac{2\pi}{|\omega_0|}.\end{aligned}​ejω0​(t+T)=ejω0​t⟺ejω0​T=1⟺ω0​T=2π⟺T0​=∣ω0​∣2π​.​

A continuous complex exponential (or sinusoid) is always periodic, for any ω0≠0\omega_0\ne0ω0​=0.

Discrete sinusoids and periodicity

In discrete time we only keep the values at integers:

x[n]=cos⁡(ω0n).x[n]=\cos(\omega_0n).x[n]=cos(ω0​n).

A discrete signal is periodic with period NNN if x[n+N]=x[n]x[n+N]=x[n]x[n+N]=x[n] for all nnn, with NNN a positive integer. The continuous cosine repeats every 2πω0\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}ω0​2π​, so the samples repeat after any multiple of it that happens to be an integer:

N=m⋅2πω0  must be an integer for some integer m  ⟺  ω02π=mN is rational.\begin{aligned}&N=m\cdot\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}\ \text{ must be an integer for some integer } m\\[6pt]&\iff \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}=\frac mN\ \text{is rational}.\end{aligned}​N=m⋅ω0​2π​  must be an integer for some integer m⟺2πω0​​=Nm​ is rational.​

Test. cos⁡(ω0n)\cos(\omega_0 n)cos(ω0​n) is periodic only if 2πω0\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega_0}ω0​2π​ is rational. Write 2πω0=Nm\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=\dfrac Nmω0​2π​=mN​ in lowest terms; then NNN is the fundamental period. The phase does not affect the period.

Examples

  • cos⁡2t\cos 2tcos2t is periodic, but cos⁡2n\cos 2ncos2n is not. The continuous period is T0=2π2=πT_0=\frac{2\pi}{2}=\piT0​=22π​=π, which is not an integer, and no integer multiple of π\piπ is an integer either. The samples never repeat exactly.
  • cos⁡2π5n\cos\frac{2\pi}{5}ncos52π​n repeats every 5 samples. After N=5N=5N=5 samples the angle has increased by 2π2\pi2π.
  • 3sin⁡57n3\sin\frac{5}{7}n3sin75​n is not periodic. 2πω0=2π5/7=14π5\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=\dfrac{2\pi}{5/7}=\dfrac{14\pi}{5}ω0​2π​=5/72π​=514π​, which is irrational, so no integer NNN works.
  • 2cos⁡(16π63n+π3)2\cos\left(\frac{16\pi}{63}n+\frac\pi3\right)2cos(6316π​n+3π​) has fundamental period 63. 2πω0=2π16π/63=638=Nm\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=\dfrac{2\pi}{16\pi/63}=\dfrac{63}{8}=\dfrac Nmω0​2π​=16π/632π​=863​=mN​, so N=63N=63N=63 and m=8m=8m=8: after 8 cycles of the underlying cosine, the samples land exactly 63 steps later. The phase π3\frac\pi33π​ plays no part.

Exam pointers

  • Always state u[0]=1u[0]=1u[0]=1 and δ[0]=1\delta[0]=1δ[0]=1 explicitly when proving step–impulse relations, and use the "is the spike in the window?" argument for the running sum.
  • For δ(t)=du/dt\delta(t)=du/dtδ(t)=du/dt, use the smoothed-ramp argument: pulse of height 1/Δ1/\Delta1/Δ, width Δ\DeltaΔ, area 1.
  • When differentiating piecewise signals, list every jump and turn it into an impulse.
  • Discrete periodicity: reduce 2πω0=Nm\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=\frac Nmω0​2π​=mN​ to lowest terms before quoting NNN; an irrational value means "not periodic".
